summary: Psalm 31 begins with a speaker taking refuge in Yahweh and asking to be delivered from hidden traps and enemies. The prayer moves through deep bodily grief, social rejection, and fear of conspirators, then turns again to trust: “You are my God.” It ends by praising Yahweh for hearing the speaker and by urging all who hope in Yahweh to be strong.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows how a psalm of distress can hold complaint, confession, trust, petition, praise, and public encouragement together. Within Book I of Psalms, it belongs among the David-associated prayers where crisis becomes speech addressed to God rather than silence.

context.author: The heading says, “For the Chief Musician. A Psalm by David.” In Psalms, headings connected with David may indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging; readers differ on how much historical information each heading establishes.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also adopting the Psalms for public prayer and private life.
context.date: The Psalms are an anthology formed over time; individual poems may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period, so one date for the whole book would be misleading.
context.setting: Book I of Psalms, where many David-associated poems speak from danger, grief, opposition, and trust. This psalm itself does not name a specific episode beyond distress, enemies, slander, and rescue.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer. The chapter is a lament and trust psalm, using images such as refuge, rock, fortress, net, hand, shelter, and shining face.

outline.heading: Taking refuge and asking rescue
outline.note: The speaker appeals to Yahweh as refuge, rock, fortress, stronghold, and redeemer, ending with the entrusting of his spirit into God’s hand.

outline.heading: Trust remembered in affliction
outline.note: The speaker rejects “lying vanities,” trusts Yahweh, and remembers that God has seen affliction and set his feet in a large place.

outline.heading: Distress, shame, and threat
outline.note: The prayer describes grief, failing strength, contempt from neighbors, abandonment by acquaintances, and plots against the speaker’s life.

outline.heading: Renewed trust and petition
outline.note: Against the pressure of enemies, the speaker says, “You are my God,” asks deliverance, and calls for lying lips to be silenced.

outline.heading: Goodness and hidden shelter
outline.note: The psalm widens from the speaker’s crisis to God’s goodness for those who fear him and take refuge in him.

outline.heading: Praise after being heard
outline.note: The speaker blesses Yahweh for marvelous loving kindness and admits that even a fearful cry of being cut off was heard.

outline.heading: Call to love and courage
outline.note: The closing turns to the faithful, urging love for Yahweh, warning the arrogant, and encouraging all who hope in Yahweh.

keyVerses.text: Into your hand I commend my spirit. You redeem me, Yahweh, God of truth.
keyVerses.why: This line gathers the psalm’s trust into one image: the speaker places life in God’s hand while naming Yahweh as redeemer and God of truth.

keyVerses.text: Have mercy on me, Yahweh, for I am in distress. My eye, my soul, and my body waste away with grief.
keyVerses.why: This verse anchors the chapter’s lament. The distress is not abstract; it touches sight, inner life, and body.

keyVerses.text: But I trust in you, Yahweh. I said, “You are my God.”
keyVerses.why: After the description of slander and plots, this verse marks the turn back to trust without pretending the danger is gone.

keyVerses.text: Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all you who hope in Yahweh.
keyVerses.why: The psalm ends by turning one person’s rescue and prayer into encouragement for a wider community.

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The heading identifies the psalm as “by David,” but Davidic headings can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging. The poem itself speaks in the first person as someone surrounded by enemies, grief, and social rejection. It can be read as an individual prayer that later worshiping communities could also take up.

questions.question: What does “For the Chief Musician” mean here?
questions.answer: The phrase appears in the heading of the psalm. Psalm headings may name performers, genres, tunes, instruments, occasions, or collections, but the exact ancient performance details are often uncertain. Here it signals that the poem belongs to a worship or musical setting, without letting readers reconstruct the full performance.

questions.question: Why does the psalm use so many shelter images?
questions.answer: The speaker calls Yahweh a refuge, strong rock, house of defense, rock, fortress, and stronghold. These images fit the pressure described later: secret nets, enemies, persecution, slander, and plots to take his life. The point is not one literal building or cliff, but repeated language for protection when the speaker feels exposed.

questions.question: What is the “net” in verse 4?
questions.answer: The verse says enemies have laid a net secretly for the speaker. In this poem the net is an image of hidden danger or entrapment, not a described historical device. The chapter does not identify who set it or what exact situation it refers to.

questions.question: Does verse 10 mean the speaker thinks all suffering is caused by sin?
questions.answer: No. Verse 10 says, “My strength fails because of my iniquity,” so this speaker includes his own wrongdoing within this prayer. But the chapter also describes enemies, slander, plots, and social rejection, so it does not reduce every part of the suffering to one cause. The responsible reading is to say what this psalm says about this speaker, not to turn it into a rule for every sufferer.

questions.question: Why does the speaker ask that the wicked be silent in Sheol?
questions.answer: This is one of the psalm’s judgment requests. The speaker asks not only to be rescued but for lying lips and wicked speech to be stopped. Readers differ over how to pray such lines today: some hear them as handing judgment to God rather than taking revenge, while others struggle with their severity. The line should first be read as part of an ancient lament from someone facing slander and threat.

questions.question: What does “My times are in your hand” mean in the flow of the psalm?
questions.answer: The speaker has already said, “Into your hand I commend my spirit,” and now says that his times are in God’s hand. In context, this is a statement of trust while enemies and persecutors are still present. It does not erase danger; it places the speaker’s life and future before Yahweh while asking for deliverance.

questions.question: Why does the psalm move from “I” to “all you his saints”?
questions.answer: Most of the psalm is one speaker’s prayer, but the ending addresses a wider group. After saying that Yahweh heard his petitions, the speaker calls Yahweh’s faithful ones to love, hope, strength, and courage. The personal testimony becomes communal encouragement.

questions.question: How should readers handle later Christian use of “Into your hand I commend my spirit”?
questions.answer: Psalm 31:5 belongs first to this psalm’s prayer of trust and rescue. Later Christian readers connect the wording with Jesus’s final words in Luke, but that later reception should not replace the verse’s role here. In Psalm 31, the line is spoken by a distressed worshiper entrusting life to Yahweh, “God of truth.”

glossary.def: A place of protection. In this psalm the speaker takes refuge in Yahweh while asking to be delivered from enemies and shame.
A secure place or defense. The speaker uses it for Yahweh in verse 4, after asking to be pulled from a secretly laid net.
The translation’s phrase for God’s loyal mercy or steadfast care in this chapter. The speaker rejoices in it, asks to be saved in it, and later praises Yahweh for showing it.
The realm of the dead in biblical language. Here the speaker asks that the wicked be silent there, as part of a plea for lying and hostile speech to stop.
